styles.ingredients: Cider apples from the respective delimited regions; the specification permits some practices the AOCs forbid, and juice from concentrate is restricted rather than banned outright.
styles.comments: The IGP tier exists to give regional producers a protected name without the full AOC constraint on keeving, variety and yield. Practically, an IGP Normandy cider may be filtered, force-carbonated and pasteurised where an AOC Pays d'Auge may not. Also registered: Cidre Cotentin AOP, and the Calvados appellations (Calvados, Calvados Pays d'Auge, Calvados Domfrontais) which govern the distilled product made from these ciders — see the Spirits edition.
styles.history: France protected the wider regional names as cider production industrialised in the later 20th century.

styles.name: DOP Sidra de Asturias
styles.impression: Bone-dry, still, funky, high-acid Asturian cider — the one that must be poured from a height to work at all.
styles.ingredients: Apples of the 76 approved Asturian varieties, classed as sweet, sharp, bittersharp, bittersweet and bitter, grown and pressed within Asturias. No added sugar or water.
styles.comments: DOP registered in 2005. Fermented dry by indigenous yeast in chestnut or stainless tanks and bottled flat, without added carbonation and usually without filtration — malolactic conversion is normal and contributes much of the character. The escanciado pour, from arm's length above the glass into a wide vessel, aerates the cider and briefly raises a spritz that the still bottle otherwise lacks; only a few centilitres are poured at a time and the last of the glass is discarded. Expect high volatile acidity and ethyl acetate relative to any other cider tradition — sought, not faulted, within limits. A separate sidra espumosa (sparkling) category exists within the DOP.
styles.history: Asturias claims the oldest continuous cider culture in Spain; the llagar and the sidrería are cultural institutions, and the tradition was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2024.
styles.tags: spain, DOP, dry, still, wild-fermented, high-acid, protected-name

styles.name: DOP Euskal Sagardoa (Basque Cider)
styles.impression: The Basque counterpart: dry, sharp, lightly funky, drunk straight from the barrel at the sagardotegi.
styles.ingredients: Apples of approved Basque varieties — Errezil, Txalaka, Goikoetxea, Moko and others — grown in the Basque Autonomous Community.
styles.comments: DOP registered in 2016. Requires 100% Basque fruit and production within the territory; sagardoa is fermented dry, unfiltered and still. The txotx ritual — the barrel tap opened and cider caught in the glass on a thin jet — serves the same aerating purpose as the Asturian escanciado. Higher malic acid than most cider traditions, with the tart, mineral, slightly acetic profile that pairs with the fixed sagardotegi menu of cod omelette, cod with peppers, and chuleta.
styles.history: Basque cider provisioned the whaling and cod fleets of the North Atlantic; the vitamin C in unpasteurised cider is credited with holding scurvy off on long voyages.
styles.tags: spain, basque, DOP, dry, still, wild-fermented, protected-name

styles.name: UK 'Cider' for Duty Purposes
styles.impression: The legal floor almost nobody expects: 35% juice, and the rest can be water and sugar.
styles.ingredients: Fermented apple or pear juice, from fresh juice or concentrate, at a minimum of 35% of the finished volume. Sugar, water, colouring within limits, and permitted additives make up the rest.
styles.comments: Under the Alcoholic Liquor Duties Act 1979 and HMRC Notice 162, a product below 35% juice is taxed as made-wine rather than cider — the 35% figure was set in 2010 to stop the lowest-juice products claiming the favourable cider rate. Cider duty applies between 1.2% and 8.5% ABV; above 8.5% the product is charged as made-wine. This is the reason a great deal of British supermarket cider sits at exactly 4.5% and contains a minority of apple. It is also why 'fruit ciders' with added flavouring frequently fall outside the cider class altogether. None of this constrains a producer making full-juice cider; it simply means the word alone tells the drinker very little.
styles.history: The 35% threshold and the 8.5% ceiling were both introduced as anti-avoidance measures rather than as quality standards.

styles.name: PGI West Country Traditional Cider / Perry
styles.impression: Full-juice West Country cider from true cider varieties — tannic, farmhouse, a world away from the duty minimum.
styles.ingredients: Fresh apple juice from cider apple varieties grown in the defined West Country counties, at a far higher juice content than the duty floor — the PGI specification sets a 90% minimum — with no concentrate.
styles.comments: The PGI protects the traditional product against the low-juice mainstream that shares its name. Fermentation is by indigenous or pitched yeast, often slow and cool, in oak or in tank; the defining flavour contribution is the tannin of true cider apples (Dabinett, Yarlington Mill, Kingston Black, Michelin, Somerset Redstreak) which are astringent and largely inedible fresh. Sold still or lightly sparkling, dry to medium. A parallel Three Counties registration covers Herefordshire, Gloucestershire and Worcestershire cider and perry.
styles.history: Registered under the EU quality schemes and retained in the UK scheme after 2021.
styles.examples: West Country farmhouse cider and traditional perry
styles.tags: uk, PGI, full-juice, tannic, farmhouse, protected-name

styles.name: Traditional Scrumpy / Farmhouse Cider
styles.impression: Still, cloudy, dry and rough-edged — the unprotected traditional product the PGIs were written around.
styles.ingredients: Whole-juice cider apples, wild-fermented, unfiltered, unpasteurised, no added sugar or water.
styles.comments: 'Scrumpy' has no legal definition at all; it is a West Country word for rough farm cider. Characteristically fermented to complete dryness by the orchard's own yeast, left unfiltered, and sold still from the barrel. Expect noticeable acetic and phenolic character, occasional mousiness from Brettanomyces or lactic bacteria, and considerable batch variation. Farmgate producers below the 70 hL annual threshold have historically been exempt from cider duty registration in the UK — the exemption underpinning the small-scale tradition, though it has been subject to repeated review.
styles.history: The medieval and early-modern default drink of the cider counties, paid partly as agricultural wages until the truck system was outlawed.
styles.examples: Farmgate cider across Somerset, Devon, Herefordshire
styles.tags: uk, traditional, wild-fermented, dry, unfiltered, no-legal-definition

styles.name: Irish Cider
styles.impression: Regulated by strength and duty like the UK, dominated commercially by a single large-scale style.
styles.ingredients: Fermented apple juice; concentrate and sugar permitted.
styles.comments: Irish Revenue charges cider and perry by ABV band with no compositional minimum comparable to the UK's 35% juice rule written into the duty definition in the same terms. The commercial category is defined in practice by Tipperary-grown dessert and culinary fruit rather than by tannic cider varieties, producing a sweeter, lower-tannin, higher-acid cider served over ice. A small full-juice artisan sector works with traditional varieties.
styles.history: Commercial Irish cider scaled rapidly from the 1930s around a single dominant producer.

styles.name: US 'Hard Cider' Tax Class (26 U.S.C. §5041)
styles.impression: A narrow tax box: apples and pears only, low carbonation, under 8.5% — step outside any one of those and it is taxed as wine.
styles.ingredients: Derived primarily from apples, apple juice concentrate, pears or pear juice concentrate and water. No fruit other than apple or pear, and no fruit flavouring other than apple or pear.
styles.comments: The hard cider tax rate applies to products of at least 0.5% and less than 8.5% ABV containing no more than 0.64 grams of carbon dioxide per 100 millilitres. The CO2 ceiling was raised from 0.392 g/100 mL by the PATH Act of 2015, which had until then pushed many naturally-conditioned ciders into the sparkling-wine rate — a tax cliff of several dollars per gallon that materially shaped what American cideries could afford to make. Add cherries, hops or spice and the product leaves the hard cider class for the wine rates. Production is regulated under 27 CFR Part 24 as a winery operation, not a brewery, so cideries hold winery permits.
styles.history: The 2015 amendment is the single most consequential piece of US cider legislation of the modern era.

styles.name: US Cider Labelling & Standards of Fill (27 CFR Part 24)
styles.impression: The labelling half: which ciders need federal label approval, and what they may claim.
styles.ingredients: Not prescribed.
styles.comments: Ciders at 7% ABV or above fall under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act and require a Certificate of Label Approval from the TTB; those below 7% are regulated for labelling by the FDA instead, which requires an ingredient list and nutrition labelling that TTB-regulated products do not — one reason many American ciders sit at exactly 6.9% or jump to 7%. Amelioration rules limit the addition of water and sugar; a cider ameliorated beyond the permitted limit cannot carry a varietal or appellation claim. State law adds a further layer, with several states defining cider separately for retail-licence purposes.
styles.history: The split jurisdiction at 7% is an artefact of the FAA Act's definition of 'wine' rather than a deliberate cider policy.

styles.name: PGI Cidre de Glace du Québec (Ice Cider)
styles.impression: Cold-concentrated apple juice fermented to a dense, sweet, high-acid dessert cider — Quebec's signature contribution.
styles.ingredients: Quebec-grown apples only. Concentration achieved solely by natural cold, by either cryoconcentration (juice pressed in autumn, then frozen outdoors over winter and the concentrate drawn off) or cryoextraction (apples left on the tree to freeze and pressed while frozen). No added sugar, water, alcohol, colouring or flavouring.
styles.comments: PGI granted 30 December 2014. The specification requires apples pressed within the harvest window running to 1 March, a pre-fermentation sugar concentration reached only through natural freezing — in practice around 30 °Brix or more — a finished alcohol of 9% to 13% ABV derived entirely from the apple's own sugars, and a residual sugar minimum of 130 g/L. Total acidity is high, typically 8–12 g/L as malic, which is what keeps a wine of that sweetness from cloying. Certification is audited by an independent body under CARTV.
styles.history: Developed in Quebec from the late 1980s in conscious analogy to ice wine, and now the province's most exported artisanal product.
styles.examples: Quebec ice cider from certified producers
styles.tags: canada, quebec, PGI, ice-cider, dessert, cryoconcentration, protected-name

styles.name: PGI Cidre de Feu du Québec (Fire Cider)
styles.impression: The mirror image of ice cider — juice concentrated by heat rather than cold, giving caramel and cooked-fruit depth.
styles.ingredients: Quebec-grown apples; juice concentrated by evaporation over heat before fermentation. No added sugar, water or flavouring.
styles.comments: Recognised as a PGI in 2021, making Quebec the only jurisdiction with protected designations for both directions of natural concentration. Heat concentration drives Maillard and caramelisation reactions the freezing route cannot, so fire cider tends toward toffee, baked apple and dried fruit where ice cider stays fresh and bright. Alcohol and residual sugar thresholds parallel the ice cider standard.
styles.history: Adapted from the maple-syrup evaporator tradition already embedded in Quebec agriculture.
styles.examples: Quebec fire cider from certified producers
styles.tags: canada, quebec, PGI, dessert, thermal-concentration, protected-name

styles.name: Hessischer Apfelwein (PGI)
styles.impression: Frankfurt's dry, sharp, still apple wine — served from the Bembel into the ribbed Geripptes glass.
styles.ingredients: Apples from the Hessen region, predominantly sharp culinary and traditional varieties rather than tannic cider apples; fermented fully dry. Historically Speierling (service tree) fruit was added for tannin and clarification.
styles.comments: Registered as a Protected Geographical Indication. German Apfelwein is defined in food law as a fermented apple product and is conventionally dry, still and pale, with high malic acid and very little tannin — closer to Asturian sidra in acidity than to English cider in structure, but without the funk. Sold as sauergespritzter (cut with sparkling water) or süßgespritzter (cut with lemonade) as a matter of course. Related registered names include Bayerischer Apfelwein and Schwäbischer Most.
styles.history: Frankfurt's apple wine culture is documented from the 16th century; the Sachsenhausen taverns are its centre.
styles.examples: Frankfurt Apfelwein from Sachsenhausen and the Hessen orchards
styles.tags: germany, PGI, dry, still, high-acid, protected-name

styles.name: Austrian Most / Mostviertel Birnenmost
styles.impression: Lower Austria's farmhouse pear and apple most — dry, tart, lightly tannic, from vast standard-tree orchards.
styles.ingredients: Perry pears (Speckbirne, Dorschbirne, Landlbirne) and apples from the Mostviertel and Steiermark standard orchards.
styles.comments: 'Most' in Austria and southern Germany denotes both unfermented juice and the fermented product depending on region and context, which causes endless confusion; Austrian Birnenmost is fermented. The Mostviertel holds one of Europe's largest concentrations of standard perry pear trees, and Mostbarone producer certification applies quality criteria above the legal minimum. Typically drier and more tannic than German Apfelwein.
styles.history: The Mostviertel takes its name from the drink; the Moststraße links the producing farms.
styles.tags: austria, perry, pear, dry, farmhouse, regional

styles.name: Keeving / Défécation (Méthode Ancestrale)
styles.impression: The technique behind every naturally sweet French cider: starve the yeast, stall the ferment, condition in bottle.
styles.ingredients: Low-nitrogen juice from tannic cider apples; calcium (naturally present or added as calcium chloride) and pectin methylesterase, either endogenous or added, to form the gel.
styles.comments: Pectin methylesterase de-esterifies the juice's pectin; the freed carboxyl groups bind calcium and form a gel that floats on carbon dioxide from the earliest fermentation, carrying the nitrogenous nutrients and suspended solids into a brown cap. Racking the clear juice from beneath it leaves a fermentation so nutrient-poor it stalls with 30–50 g/L of sugar remaining, which then produces natural bottle carbonation without dosage. Requires genuinely low-nitrogen fruit — orchard fertilisation defeats it — and is temperature-sensitive, generally needing 4–10 °C. This is not a legal designation but it is the practice several of the appellations above require, and the reason a true AOC cider is sweet without any sugar being added.
styles.history: A Norman and Breton practice of long standing, adopted by English producers from the late 20th century.
styles.examples: AOC Pays d'Auge, AOP Cornouaille, keeved English ciders

styles.name: Sidra Natural (Still, Wild, Unfiltered)
styles.impression: The Atlantic method: ferment dry, leave it alone, pour it hard.
styles.ingredients: Whole apple juice, indigenous yeast, no additions, no filtration, no forced carbonation.
styles.comments: The shared technical description behind Asturian sidra natural, Basque sagardoa and their Latin American descendants. Fermentation runs to complete dryness, malolactic conversion follows and softens the malic acid into lactic, and the cider is bottled flat and unfiltered. The high-pour serving ritual is functional: aeration volatilises esters and briefly raises a foam that carries aroma, and the cider flattens again within a minute, which is why only a small measure is poured at a time. Volatile acidity is higher than any other tradition would tolerate.
styles.history: Carried to Argentina, Chile and Mexico by Asturian and Basque emigration, where the tradition persists.
styles.examples: Asturian and Basque sidra natural; South American Asturian-diaspora cider
styles.tags: method, dry, still, wild-fermented, unfiltered, technique

legalStandards.title: Fortified, Aromatised & Traditional Fermented Beverages
legalStandards.attribution: Legal definitions and protected-designation rules for fermented and fortified drinks that fall outside beer, mead and cider judging guidelines: EU Regulation 2019/787 and 251/2014 (aromatised wine products), Portuguese and Spanish DO/DOC statutes, Japan's Liquor Tax Act and the Seishu standard, and Mexico's NOM-070 family. Figures are legal limits, not sensory targets. Traditional beverages with no statutory definition are marked as such and described from ethnographic and industry sources.

styles.name: Port
styles.impression: Sweet fortified wine from the Douro, arrested mid-ferment by grape spirit so natural sugar remains.
styles.ingredients: Permitted Douro varieties — Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz, Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão and others; fortified with aguardente vínica at ~77% ABV.
styles.comments: DOC Porto (IVDP): grapes grown in the demarcated Douro region — the world's first demarcated wine region (1756). Fermentation is stopped by adding grape spirit, leaving residual sugar; finished at 19–22% ABV. Styles: Ruby, Reserve, LBV (Late Bottled Vintage, 4–6 years), Tawny with indication of age (10/20/30/40 years), Colheita (single-vintage tawny), and Vintage (declared years, ~2 years in cask then bottle-aged).

styles.name: Sherry
styles.impression: Andalusian fortified wine spanning bone-dry biologically-aged styles to intensely sweet.
styles.ingredients: Palomino for dry styles; Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel for sweet.
styles.comments: DO Jerez-Xérès-Sherry: from the albariza soils of the Marco de Jerez triangle, matured under the solera fractional-blending system. Biologically aged styles develop under a film of flor yeast: Fino and Manzanilla (~15–15.5% ABV, the flor cannot survive higher). Oxidatively aged: Oloroso (17–22%), Amontillado (flor then oxidative), Palo Cortado. Sweet: PX, which can exceed 400 g/L residual sugar.
styles.history: The solera system and flor ageing are found almost nowhere else in the wine world.

styles.name: Madeira
styles.impression: Portuguese island wine deliberately heated and oxidised — practically indestructible once opened.
styles.ingredients: Sercial (driest), Verdelho, Bual, Malmsey (sweetest); Tinta Negra for most volume.
styles.comments: DOP Madeira: fortified and then heat-aged, either by estufagem (heated tanks, ~45–50 °C for ≥3 months) or canteiro (slow ambient cask ageing in warm lofts, years). The heating is what makes the wine effectively immune to further oxidation. Frasqueira/Garrafeira denotes ≥20 years canteiro from a single vintage.
styles.history: The style was discovered accidentally when barrels crossed the tropics as ship ballast and improved en route.

styles.name: Marsala
styles.impression: Sicilian fortified wine, dry to sweet, in gold, amber and ruby.
styles.comments: DOC Marsala (1969): from Grillo, Catarratto, Inzolia (gold/amber) or red varieties (ruby). Classified by ageing: Fine (≥1 year), Superiore (≥2), Superiore Riserva (≥4), Vergine/Soleras (≥5, unsweetened), Vergine Stravecchio (≥10).

styles.name: Vermouth
styles.impression: Aromatised wine defined by wormwood.
styles.ingredients: At least 75% wine, flavoured with species of Artemisia.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 251/2014: an aromatised wine whose flavouring necessarily includes Artemisia species; wine content ≥75%; alcohol 14.5–22% ABV; may be sweetened and coloured. Vermouth di Torino holds a protected geographical indication requiring Italian wine and Artemisia grown in Piedmont where possible.

styles.name: Sake (Seishu)
styles.impression: Japanese rice beverage produced by multiple parallel fermentation — kōji saccharifies starch while yeast ferments simultaneously, reaching high alcohol without distillation.
styles.ingredients: Rice, water, kōji (Aspergillus oryzae), yeast; brewer's alcohol permitted in some grades.
styles.comments: Japan's Liquor Tax Act defines seishu: made from rice, rice kōji and water, filtered, and not exceeding 22% ABV. Grades are set by rice-polishing ratio (seimaibuai) and whether distilled alcohol is added — Junmai (no added alcohol), Honjozo (≤10% added alcohol, ≤70% polish), Ginjo (≤60% polish), Daiginjo (≤50% polish). Namazake is unpasteurised; nigori is coarsely filtered.
styles.comparison: Often called 'rice wine', but the parallel saccharification makes it closer in process to beer than to wine.

styles.name: Huangjiu (Chinese Yellow Wine)
styles.impression: Amber Chinese grain beverage, the fermented ancestor of baijiu's raw material.
styles.ingredients: Glutinous rice, millet or wheat, fermented with qū starter.
styles.comments: Governed by Chinese GB/T 13662 standards, classified by residual sugar (dry, semi-dry, semi-sweet, sweet). Shaoxing huangjiu holds a protected geographical indication; aged examples (chen nian) are prized and widely used in cooking.

styles.name: Makgeolli / Takju
styles.impression: Cloudy, lightly sparkling Korean rice brew.
styles.ingredients: Rice (or wheat), nuruk starter culture, water.
styles.comments: Korean Liquor Tax Act classes unrefined rice brews as takju; makgeolli is the common name. Typically 6–8% ABV, unfiltered, often still actively fermenting — traditionally served shaken to resuspend the sediment.

styles.name: Pulque
styles.impression: Viscous, tangy, milky Mesoamerican beverage from fermented agave sap — not distilled.
styles.ingredients: Aguamiel, the sap of mature maguey (Agave salmiana, A. americana), fermented by a bacterial and yeast consortium including Zymomonas mobilis.
styles.comments: Pre-Hispanic in origin and sacred in Aztec practice. There is no denomination of origin; it is regulated only as a general fermented beverage. Because it does not keep or transport well, it is still largely a local product of the Mexican central highlands.

styles.name: Tepache
styles.impression: Lightly fermented Mexican pineapple refresher, mildly alcoholic.
styles.ingredients: Pineapple rind and flesh, piloncillo, water, spices; wild fermentation.
styles.comments: No statutory definition — a traditional home and street beverage, typically fermented only a few days. Commercial versions vary from effectively non-alcoholic to hard-seltzer strength.

styles.name: Palm Wine / Toddy
styles.impression: Sap of palm trees fermenting spontaneously, often within hours of tapping.
styles.ingredients: Sap of oil, date, coconut or raffia palms.
styles.comments: No unified legal standard; regulated locally across West Africa, South and Southeast Asia. Fermentation begins immediately on tapping via wild yeasts already present in the sap, so strength climbs through the day and the drink is consumed fresh. Distilled onward it becomes arrack or ogogoro.

styles.name: Tej (Ethiopian Honey Wine)
styles.impression: Ethiopian and Eritrean honey wine bittered with gesho — effectively a hopped mead.
styles.ingredients: Honey, water, and gesho (Rhamnus prinoides) leaves and stems as the bittering agent.
styles.comments: No formal legal standard outside local practice. Distinct from Western mead in that gesho supplies both bitterness and, historically, some of the fermentation microflora. A lower-strength, honey-lean version is called berz.
styles.comparison: BJCP judges a comparable product under Specialty Mead, but tej's gesho bittering has no direct Western analogue.

styles.name: Kumis & Airag
styles.impression: Fermented mare's milk of the Central Asian steppe — sour, effervescent, very low in alcohol.
styles.ingredients: Raw mare's milk fermented by lactobacilli and lactose-fermenting yeasts (notably Kluyveromyces marxianus).
styles.comments: No international standard; produced traditionally across Mongolia (airag), Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Brewing yeast cannot ferment lactose at all, which is precisely why this tradition depends on Kluyveromyces — the same species catalogued in the yeast database under wild and heritage strains.
styles.tags: kumis, airag, mare milk, kluyveromyces, lactose

legalStandards.title: Sake (Seishu): Legal Classification & Production Designations
legalStandards.attribution: Sake has no judging style guidelines in the BJCP sense, but it has something stricter: a labelling standard with the force of tax law. This edition follows Japan's Liquor Tax Act definition of seishu and the National Tax Agency's Standard for Manufacturing Methods and Quality Labelling of Sake (清酒の製法品質表示基準), which defines the eight tokutei meishōshu — 'special designation' — grades by rice polishing ratio (seimaibuai), koji proportion and whether brewer's alcohol is added. Alongside those it collects the production-method and treatment terms (kimoto, yamahai, namazake, genshu, nigori) that are separately regulated or conventionally defined, and the geographical indications. Figures are legal thresholds, not sensory targets. Nihonshu-do (Sake Meter Value) and san-do (acidity) are given as typical commercial ranges for calculator reference, not as requirements. Check the current NTA notification before relying on any of this commercially.

styles.name: Seishu (清酒) — Refined Sake
styles.impression: The statutory category that everything below sits inside: rice, koji and water, fermented and then filtered.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water; optionally sake lees and, within limits, distilled alcohol and other permitted materials whose combined weight must not exceed the weight of the rice used.
styles.comments: Japan's Liquor Tax Act (酒税法) defines seishu as an alcoholic beverage of not more than 22% ABV made by fermenting rice, rice koji and water and then filtering (漉す) the resulting mash. The filtration requirement is decisive: an unfiltered rice ferment is legally doburoku, taxed as 'other brewed liquor', not as seishu — which is why nigorizake must be coarsely strained rather than left whole. Commercial seishu is typically 15–16% ABV after dilution; genshu (undiluted) runs 17–20%. Brewing sake at home is illegal in Japan under the same Act, a restriction with no equivalent for beer or wine in most other countries.
styles.history: The filtration clause dates from the Meiji-era tax reforms that made sake excise a pillar of state revenue — by some accounts approaching a third of national tax income in the 1890s.

styles.name: Futsūshu (普通酒) — Ordinary Sake
styles.impression: Everything that does not qualify for a special designation — roughly two-thirds of all sake made.
styles.ingredients: Rice, koji, water, and distilled alcohol in quantities above the tokutei meishōshu limit; sugars, acidulants and amino acids (glutamate) are permitted within the statutory cap.
styles.comments: Futsūshu is a residual category, not a quality claim: it covers sake that fails any tokutei meishōshu requirement, most often because the polishing ratio is above 70% or because alcohol addition exceeds 10% of the white-rice weight. The total weight of added materials may not exceed 50% of the rice weight. Much of it is perfectly sound everyday drinking, and some sanzōshu-derived styles are historically important, but the label carries no minimum.
styles.history: Sanzōshu ('triple-multiplied sake'), heavily extended with alcohol and sugar, was a wartime and post-war rice-shortage expedient whose reputation still shadows the category.
styles.examples: Most cup sake, table sake and much of what is served warm in restaurants

styles.name: Junmai-shu (純米酒)
styles.impression: Rice, koji, water. Nothing added — typically fuller, more savoury and more acidic than its alcohol-added counterpart.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water only. Koji rice must be at least 15% of the total rice weight. No minimum polishing ratio applies, but the seimaibuai must be stated on the label.
styles.comments: Until 2004 junmai required a polishing ratio of 70% or better; that floor was removed and replaced with a disclosure requirement, so a modern junmai may be milled to any degree provided the figure is declared. Typical Sake Meter Value −2 to +5, acidity 1.4–1.8 — generally higher acidity and more umami than aruten (alcohol-added) sake at the same grade, because ethanol addition selectively extracts lighter aromatics and dilutes acidity.
styles.history: The junmai revival from the 1970s onward, led by producers rejecting post-war alcohol extension, created the modern premium market.
styles.examples: Widely produced by essentially every kura

styles.name: Tokubetsu Junmai-shu (特別純米酒)
styles.impression: Junmai with a declared special something — usually a 60% polish, sometimes a named rice or method.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water; koji rice at least 15%; seimaibuai of 60% or better, OR a special production method that must be described on the label.
styles.comments: 'Tokubetsu' (special) is the standard's one genuinely open-ended term. A brewery may claim it by milling to 60% — which would also qualify the sake as junmai ginjo — or by some other declared distinction such as an all-Yamada Nishiki grist, extended low-temperature fermentation, or a particular water source. Producers often choose tokubetsu junmai over junmai ginjo for a 60%-milled sake whose character is fuller and less aromatic than the ginjo archetype, since the ginjo name carries a flavour expectation the sake would not meet.
styles.history: Introduced with the 1990 designation system as a bridge between the plain and ginjo tiers.

styles.name: Junmai Ginjo-shu (純米吟醸酒)
styles.impression: Aromatic, refined, fruit-forward sake made without added alcohol — melon, pear, banana, white flowers.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water; koji rice at least 15%; seimaibuai 60% or better; produced by ginjo-zukuri.
styles.comments: Ginjo-zukuri is defined in the standard as careful brewing at low temperature to produce a distinctive aroma and clean flavour — deliberately qualitative language covering a real technical practice: fermentation held around 8–12 °C for four to five weeks, with yeasts selected for ginjo-ka. The characteristic esters are ethyl caproate (apple, melon) and isoamyl acetate (banana, pear); their balance is largely a yeast choice, with Association No. 9 (Kumamoto) and No. 1801 among the classic aromatic strains. Typical SMV −1 to +5, acidity 1.2–1.6.
styles.history: Ginjo brewing was refined through 20th-century national appraisal competitions (Zenkoku Shinshu Kanpyōkai) before reaching the commercial market in the 1980s.
styles.examples: The backbone of the export premium market

styles.name: Junmai Daiginjo-shu (純米大吟醸酒)
styles.impression: The top of the junmai ladder: at least half the rice grain milled away, no added alcohol, maximum aromatic refinement.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water; koji rice at least 15%; seimaibuai 50% or better; ginjo-zukuri.
styles.comments: The 50% threshold is a floor, not a target — competition sake is routinely milled to 40%, 35% or beyond, and a handful of releases go under 20%, at which point most of the purchased rice has become animal feed and rice flour. Milling removes the outer layers rich in protein, fat and minerals, leaving the starchy shinpaku core; the result is cleaner and more aromatic but also less structured, which is why more milling is not straightforwardly better. Sake rice varieties bred for a large central shinpaku — Yamada Nishiki, Omachi, Gohyakumangoku, Miyama Nishiki — tolerate deep polishing without shattering.
styles.history: Yamada Nishiki, crossed in 1923 and named in 1936, remains the benchmark rice for this tier.

styles.name: Honjozo-shu (本醸造酒)
styles.impression: Lighter, drier and crisper than junmai at the same price — a small alcohol addition used as a technique, not an extender.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji, water and distilled alcohol; koji rice at least 15%; seimaibuai 70% or better; added alcohol limited to 10% of the weight of the polished white rice.
styles.comments: The 10% cap is what separates honjozo from futsūshu, and the distinction matters: added at the end of fermentation, a small quantity of neutral distillate lifts aroma compounds out of the lees during pressing, lightens the body and improves stability. It is a legitimate brewing tool with a long pre-war history, not dilution — the sanzōshu practice that gave alcohol addition a bad name involved several times this quantity plus sugar. Honjozo is the classic warming sake; typical SMV +2 to +7.
styles.history: The technique descends from Edo-period 'hashira-jōchū', in which shōchū was added to the mash to prevent spoilage.
styles.examples: The traditional everyday premium grade in Japan

styles.name: Tokubetsu Honjozo-shu (特別本醸造酒)
styles.impression: Honjozo with a declared distinction — normally a 60% polish.
styles.ingredients: As honjozo, but seimaibuai 60% or better, OR a special production method described on the label. Added alcohol still capped at 10% of white-rice weight.
styles.comments: Mirrors tokubetsu junmai exactly, one tier over. Chosen where a 60%-milled aruten sake is built for structure and drinkability rather than for ginjo aromatics.
styles.history: Introduced with the 1990 designation system.

styles.name: Ginjo-shu (吟醸酒)
styles.impression: Aromatic ginjo with a small alcohol addition — often more overtly fragrant than its junmai equivalent.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji, water, distilled alcohol; koji rice at least 15%; seimaibuai 60% or better; ginjo-zukuri; alcohol capped at 10% of white-rice weight.
styles.comments: Because ginjo esters are more soluble in ethanol than in water, the alcohol addition pulls aroma out of the pressed lees and into the bottle. A brewer chasing maximum fragrance for a competition will often make an alcohol-added daiginjo rather than a junmai one, which is why the top prizes at the national appraisal are frequently taken by aruten sake.
styles.history: Ginjo without the junmai qualifier was the original competition format.
styles.examples: Widely produced; common in national appraisal entries

styles.name: Daiginjo-shu (大吟醸酒)
styles.impression: The most technically demanding grade in the standard: 50% polish, ginjo method, small alcohol addition.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji, water, distilled alcohol; koji rice at least 15%; seimaibuai 50% or better; ginjo-zukuri; alcohol capped at 10% of white-rice weight.
styles.comments: The showpiece grade. Fermented cold and slow in small tanks, often pressed by fukurozuri — hanging the mash in bags and collecting the free-run drip without pressure — for the shizuku fraction reserved for competition. Typical SMV +3 to +5, acidity 1.1–1.4.
styles.history: Yamada Nishiki milled to 35–40% has dominated the Zenkoku Shinshu Kanpyōkai gold awards for decades.

styles.name: Sokujō-moto (速醸酛) — Fast Starter
styles.impression: The modern default: lactic acid added directly to the starter, ready in about two weeks.
styles.ingredients: Steamed rice, koji, water, cultured yeast, and food-grade lactic acid added at the outset.
styles.comments: Around 90% of all sake made today uses sokujō. Adding lactic acid up front drops the starter's pH immediately, suppressing wild organisms and letting the pitched yeast take over without the long competitive succession the traditional methods require. Clean, reproducible, and neutral in flavour contribution. Not a labelling designation — its absence is implied when neither kimoto nor yamahai is stated.
styles.history: Developed by Kinichiro Eda at the National Research Institute of Brewing around 1909 and adopted rapidly.
styles.examples: The overwhelming majority of commercial sake

styles.name: Kimoto (生酛)
styles.impression: The traditional starter, built by hand and by microbial succession — richer, more acidic, more savoury sake.
styles.ingredients: Steamed rice, koji, water and ambient microflora; no added lactic acid, no pitched yeast at the outset.
styles.comments: The rice and koji are ground to a paste with wooden poles (yama-oroshi, a labour of several hours repeated over days) to accelerate saccharification. Nitrate-reducing bacteria, then wild lactic acid bacteria, then finally yeast take the starter in succession over roughly four weeks; the accumulating lactic acid selects for alcohol-tolerant yeast. The resulting sake carries higher acidity and amino acid content, and often more lactic, nutty and gamey character. It also tends to be more robust when warmed and better suited to ageing.
styles.history: Standardised at the Nada breweries in the 17th century; nearly extinct by the late 20th, now a deliberate revival.
styles.examples: Widely used by producers pursuing a traditional or food-friendly profile

styles.name: Yamahai (山廃)
styles.impression: Kimoto without the pole-grinding — the same wild succession, a fraction of the labour.
styles.ingredients: As kimoto; no added lactic acid.
styles.comments: Short for yamaoroshi haishi — 'discontinuing the yamaoroshi'. Research at the turn of the 20th century established that the koji enzymes dissolve the rice perfectly well without mechanical mashing if the water and temperature regime is managed, making the grinding step redundant. Yamahai retains the natural lactic succession and delivers a broadly kimoto-like profile: fuller, higher acid, more umami, sometimes with a distinct earthiness. Often the choice for sake intended to be served warm.
styles.history: Developed around 1909, contemporaneously with sokujō, at the same national research institute.
styles.examples: A signature of several Ishikawa and Fukushima producers

styles.name: Bodaimoto / Mizumoto (菩提酛・水酛)
styles.impression: The oldest surviving starter method: a deliberately soured raw-rice water, made in summer.
styles.ingredients: Raw and steamed rice, water and koji; souring achieved by steeping raw rice in water until lactic bacteria acidify it (soyashi-mizu), which is then used as the brewing liquor.
styles.comments: Predates kimoto. Raw rice is steeped in water for several days at ambient summer temperature; lactic acid bacteria naturally present acidify the water sharply, and that acidified water becomes the base for the starter. The result is high acidity and a distinctly tart, sometimes yoghurt-like profile. Revived from the 1990s by a consortium of Nara brewers working from temple records.
styles.history: Documented at Shōryakuji temple in Nara in the Muromachi period; the temple is often called the birthplace of clear sake.
styles.tags: japan, shubo, historical, high-acid, revival, method

styles.name: Kijōshu (貴醸酒)
styles.impression: Sake brewed with sake instead of water — dense, sweet, amber, dessert-scaled.
styles.ingredients: Rice, koji, and finished sake substituted for part of the brewing water at the final mash addition.
styles.comments: Replacing water with sake at the last of the three staged mash additions raises the alcohol early, arresting fermentation and leaving very high residual sugar — SMV commonly −20 to −40. The result is viscous, honeyed and often deliberately aged to amber. Legally still seishu, but the substitution is a defined production style rather than a designation grade, and it is expensive because the input sake is itself a finished product.
styles.history: Developed at the National Research Institute of Brewing in 1973, reconstructing a technique described in the 10th-century Engishiki.
styles.examples: Dessert and aged bottlings from a small number of producers

styles.name: Namazake (生酒) — Unpasteurised
styles.impression: Never heated — fresher, livelier, sometimes faintly spritzy, and perishable.
styles.comments: Standard sake is pasteurised twice (hi-ire): once before storage and once at bottling. Namazake skips both and must be kept refrigerated throughout; left warm it develops namahine-ka, a stewed, cabbage-like off-character. Related partial designations: nama-chozo (unpasteurised in storage, pasteurised at bottling) and nama-zume (pasteurised before storage, bottled without a second heating). Any grade may be nama.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Only became commercially widespread once cold-chain distribution made it practical in the 1980s.
styles.examples: Seasonal shiboritate and spring nama releases

styles.name: Genshu (原酒) — Undiluted
styles.impression: Bottled at full fermentation strength, without the customary water addition.
styles.comments: Most sake finishes fermentation near 18–20% ABV — among the highest of any naturally fermented beverage, achieved by multiple parallel fermentation, in which koji enzymes saccharify starch at the same rate the yeast consumes the sugar — and is then cut with water to about 15–16%. Genshu omits that cut. Denser, warmer, more intense; often served over ice (on-za-rokku), which is one of the few sanctioned uses of dilution at the table.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: The dilution convention arose partly from tax structure and partly from the palate expectations of the domestic market.
styles.examples: Common in nama genshu seasonal releases

styles.name: Nigorizake (にごり酒) — Cloudy
styles.impression: Coarsely strained rather than clarified — white, textural, frequently sweet.
styles.comments: The legal requirement is that the mash be strained through *something*; the mesh may be coarse enough to leave substantial rice solids. That is the line between nigorizake, which is seishu, and doburoku, which is not strained at all and falls into a different tax class. Ranges from a light haze (usu-nigori) to a thick, spoonable suspension. If bottled active it may continue to ferment and build pressure — several producers ship deliberately sparkling nigori, and the bottles need careful opening.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: The visual ancestor of all sake; clear sake is the later refinement.

styles.name: Muroka (無濾過) — No Charcoal Filtration
styles.impression: Skips the activated-carbon polish, keeping colour and flavour that filtration would strip.
styles.comments: Conventional practice passes pressed sake over activated charcoal to remove colour and soften rough aromatics. Muroka omits it, leaving a faintly golden or greenish tint and a fuller, more assertive flavour. Frequently combined as muroka nama genshu — unfiltered, unpasteurised, undiluted — which is about as unmediated as commercial sake gets and is a hallmark of the modern jizake movement.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Charcoal filtration became standard in the 20th century for cosmetic consistency; muroka is a deliberate reversal.

styles.name: Koshu / Jukusei-shu (古酒・熟成酒) — Aged Sake
styles.impression: Deliberately matured — amber to brown, with sherry, mushroom, caramel and soy notes.
styles.comments: There is no statutory minimum age for the term, though the Long-Term Aged Sake Producers Association applies a three-year convention for jukusei koshu. Ageing drives Maillard chemistry between amino acids and sugars, darkening the sake and building umami; warm-aged examples develop quickly and heavily, cold-aged ones more slowly and delicately. Junmai and kijōshu age best because they carry the amino acid load to work with. Sake is otherwise conventionally treated as a fresh product with a stated brewing year (BY) rather than a vintage.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade.
styles.history: Aged sake was recorded in the Edo period, disappeared under the Meiji tax regime that charged duty at production, and returned from the 1970s.

styles.name: Sparkling Sake / Awasake (スパークリング清酒)
styles.impression: Carbonated sake, from lightly petillant nigori to bottle-fermented and disgorged.
styles.comments: Not a tax-law designation. The awasake Association applies a voluntary standard for the premium end: bottle-refermented, no added carbon dioxide, clear after disgorgement or fine filtration, minimum pressure, and made only from rice, koji and water. Below that sits a large market of low-alcohol force-carbonated products around 5–8% ABV. Bottle-conditioned nigori sits in between and is often actively fermenting in the bottle.
styles.ingredients: As per the underlying grade; secondary fermentation from residual or added sugar.
styles.history: The premium bottle-fermented category dates to the 2010s and the awasake standard to 2016.
styles.examples: Bottle-fermented awasake and commodity sparkling sake

styles.name: GI Nihonshu (日本酒) — 'Japanese Sake'
styles.impression: A national geographical indication: only sake made in Japan from Japanese rice may be called nihonshu.
styles.ingredients: Rice grown in Japan, rice koji made from Japanese rice, and water; the entire production — fermentation, pressing, filtration and bottling — carried out in Japan.
styles.comments: Designated by the National Tax Agency in December 2015. Sake brewed outside Japan, of which there is now a substantial quantity in the United States, Canada, France, Norway and elsewhere, remains legally seishu-equivalent in its own jurisdiction but cannot be labelled nihonshu for markets recognising the GI. The designation protects the word, not the method — a foreign brewer may use identical rice varieties, koji and technique.
styles.history: Part of a broader Japanese push to secure GI protection for its agricultural and beverage exports.
styles.examples: All Japan-produced sake meeting the conditions

styles.name: Regional Sake GIs (Yamagata, Hakusan, Nada, Harima…)
styles.impression: Prefectural and sub-regional designations, each with its own production specification and tasting panel.
styles.ingredients: Set by each individual GI specification — typically prescribing local water, permitted rice, production within the delimited area, and a sensory approval step.
styles.comments: GI Hakusan (Ishikawa, 2005) was the first, followed by GI Yamagata (2016) — the first covering an entire prefecture — and subsequently Nada Gogo (Hyogo), Harima, Mie, Nagano, Toyama, Saga, Yamanashi and others. Specifications commonly require that the rice and water be local, that the sake be brewed and bottled within the area, and that it pass an organoleptic assessment before the designation may be used. Because each is distinct, the GI on a label tells you the sake met a regional committee's standard, not that it belongs to a defined flavour category.
styles.history: Modelled on European wine appellation practice and administered by the National Tax Agency.
styles.examples: GI Yamagata, GI Hakusan, GI Nada Gogo

styles.name: Doburoku (どぶろく) — Unstrained Rice Brew
styles.impression: The unstrained ancestor of sake — thick, porridge-like, actively fermenting, and legally not sake at all.
styles.ingredients: Rice, rice koji and water, fermented and consumed without pressing or straining.
styles.comments: Because it is never filtered it falls outside the seishu definition and is taxed as 'other brewed liquor' (その他の醸造酒). Home production remains illegal in Japan, but designated doburoku tokku — special deregulation zones established from 2002 — allow licensed farm and inn producers to make and sell it, which has driven a rural revival. Typically served fresh, sweet-sour and lightly effervescent.
styles.history: The pre-modern village and shrine brew; suppressed as home brewing was criminalised under the Meiji tax regime.
styles.examples: Farm-inn doburoku from deregulation zones; shrine festival brews

styles.name: Amazake (甘酒) — Non-Alcoholic Koji Drink
styles.impression: Saccharified rice without fermentation — sweet, thick, and useful to brewers as a koji reference point.
styles.ingredients: Rice and rice koji held warm (around 55–60 °C) until amylases convert the starch to glucose; or, in the cheaper version, sake lees plus sugar and water.
styles.comments: Included here because it isolates the enzymatic half of sake production. Holding koji at 55–60 °C runs saccharification without yeast — the mash goes sweet and stops. It demonstrates why sake reaches such high alcohol: in the real mash the same enzymes run continuously alongside the yeast, feeding it sugar slowly enough that it is never osmotically shocked. The koji-only version is alcohol-free; the sake-lees version carries residual alcohol, typically under 1%.
styles.history: Recorded in the Nihon Shoki as amanotamuzake; a traditional summer restorative and New Year drink.

legalStandards.title: Spirits: Legal Definitions & Standards of Identity
legalStandards.attribution: Unlike beer, mead, and cider, distilled spirits have no judging style guidelines — but they do have binding legal definitions. This edition compiles the actual statutory standards of identity: the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 (UK), the Irish Whiskey Technical File, US 27 CFR Part 5 (TTB), EU Regulation 2019/787, Mexico's NOM-006/NOM-070, French AOC decrees, and equivalent national standards. Figures are the legal minima/maxima, not sensory targets. Compiled for reference; always check the current regulation for the jurisdiction you are producing in.

styles.name: Single Malt Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky distilled at a single Scottish distillery from 100% malted barley in pot stills, matured in Scotland in oak.
styles.ingredients: Water, malted barley only. No other cereals. Yeast; fermentation by endogenous enzyme systems only.
styles.comments: Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: distilled below 94.8% ABV; matured in oak casks not exceeding 700 litres, in Scotland, for at least 3 years; bottled at no less than 40% ABV. The only permitted additions are water and plain caramel colouring (E150A). Age statements must refer to the youngest whisky in the bottle.
styles.history: Protected UK geographical indication; the modern legal framework dates to the 1988 Scotch Whisky Act, consolidated in the 2009 Regulations.

styles.name: Single Grain Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: Scotch distilled at a single distillery from malted barley plus other whole cereals, typically in continuous column stills.
styles.ingredients: Water, malted barley, and whole grains of other cereals (commonly wheat or maize).
styles.comments: Same core Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 requirements as single malt — <94.8% ABV off the still, ≥3 years in oak ≤700 L in Scotland, ≥40% ABV bottling. 'Single' denotes one distillery, not one cask or one grain.

styles.name: Blended Scotch Whisky
styles.impression: A blend of one or more single malt Scotch whiskies with one or more single grain Scotch whiskies.
styles.comments: The dominant Scotch category by volume. All component whiskies must independently meet the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009. Blended Malt = malts only from multiple distilleries; Blended Grain = grains only from multiple distilleries.
styles.examples: Johnnie Walker, Chivas Regal, Famous Grouse

styles.name: Irish Whiskey
styles.impression: Whiskey distilled and matured on the island of Ireland; often triple-distilled and comparatively light.
styles.ingredients: Cereal grains; malted barley providing the enzymes.
styles.comments: Irish Whiskey Technical File (EU GI): distilled to less than 94.8% ABV; matured in wooden casks not exceeding 700 litres for at least 3 years on the island of Ireland; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Only water and plain caramel may be added.
styles.history: Protected EU geographical indication covering both the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland.

styles.name: Single Pot Still Irish Whiskey
styles.impression: The distinctive Irish style: a mixed mash of malted and unmalted barley pot-distilled at a single distillery, giving a characteristic creamy, spicy texture.
styles.ingredients: A mash of at least 30% malted barley and at least 30% unmalted barley; up to 5% other cereals permitted.
styles.comments: Defined in the Irish Whiskey Technical File. The unmalted barley — historically a response to 19th-century malt taxation — is what produces the category's signature mouthfeel.
styles.examples: Redbreast, Green Spot, Powers John's Lane

styles.name: Canadian Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky mashed, distilled and matured in Canada; historically rye-influenced and often light-bodied.
styles.comments: Canadian Food and Drug Regulations (B.02.020): mashed, distilled and aged in Canada; aged at least 3 years in small wood (≤700 L); bottled at ≥40% ABV. Uniquely, caramel and flavouring may be added — and up to 9.09% of another spirit may be blended in (the '9.09% rule'), which is why some Canadian whisky contains a small proportion of US bourbon or wine spirit.
styles.comparison: Often labelled 'rye' in Canada regardless of actual rye content, unlike US rye whiskey which requires ≥51% rye.

styles.name: Japanese Whisky
styles.impression: Whisky made in Japan, historically modelled on Scotch practice.
styles.comments: Japan had no binding legal definition until the Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association standard took effect in 2021 (voluntary, industry self-regulation): malted grain must be used, water must be extracted in Japan, saccharification/fermentation/distillation must occur at a Japanese distillery, distillation below 95% ABV, maturation ≥3 years in wooden casks ≤700 L in Japan, and bottling in Japan at ≥40% ABV. Products not meeting this may still legally be sold as Japanese-made whisky, so labels warrant scrutiny.

styles.name: Bourbon Whiskey
styles.impression: America's flagship whiskey: corn-dominant, aged in new charred oak, sweet and full.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 51% corn.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled to no more than 80% ABV (160 proof); entered into the barrel at no more than 62.5% ABV (125 proof); stored in NEW charred oak containers; bottled at no less than 40% ABV (80 proof). No colouring, flavouring or other blending materials may be added. There is no minimum ageing period for plain 'bourbon' — but see Straight Bourbon.
styles.history: Bourbon may be produced anywhere in the United States, not only Kentucky — a common misconception.
styles.examples: Buffalo Trace, Maker's Mark, Wild Turkey

styles.name: Straight Bourbon Whiskey
styles.impression: Bourbon that has met a minimum maturation period.
styles.comments: All bourbon requirements plus storage in new charred oak for at least 2 years. If aged less than 4 years, the label must carry an age statement. 'Bottled in Bond' is stricter still (Standards of Fill / 27 CFR 5.88): the product of one distillation season by one distiller at one distillery, aged ≥4 years in a federally bonded warehouse, and bottled at exactly 50% ABV (100 proof).
styles.examples: Knob Creek, Elijah Craig, Henry McKenna Bottled-in-Bond

styles.name: Rye Whiskey (US)
styles.impression: Spicier, drier counterpart to bourbon.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 51% rye.
styles.comments: Identical distillation, barrel-entry and bottling limits to bourbon (≤80% ABV distillation, ≤62.5% ABV barrel entry, new charred oak, ≥40% ABV bottling). 'Straight Rye' requires ≥2 years.
styles.comparison: Contrast Canadian 'rye', which carries no rye-content requirement.

styles.name: Corn Whiskey
styles.impression: The legal ancestor of 'moonshine' — a corn-dominant whiskey that need not see new charred oak.
styles.ingredients: Fermented mash of not less than 80% corn.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled to ≤80% ABV. Uniquely, if aged at all it must be in UNUSED uncharred oak or USED barrels, and entered at ≤62.5% ABV. It may also be sold unaged. This is the category most 'white whiskey' and commercial 'moonshine' is legally bottled under.
styles.comparison: 'Moonshine' is not itself a federal standard of identity. Commercially it is sold either as corn whiskey, as unaged whisky, or — if distilled above 95% ABV from sugar — as neutral spirits or a specialty/flavoured product.

styles.name: Tennessee Whiskey
styles.impression: Bourbon-spec whiskey charcoal-mellowed before barrelling.
styles.comments: Tennessee Code § 57-2-106 and the NAFTA/USMCA designation: must meet all bourbon requirements, be produced in Tennessee, and be filtered through maple charcoal before ageing — the Lincoln County Process. Prichard's holds a statutory exemption from the charcoal step.

styles.name: American Single Malt Whiskey
styles.impression: The newest US standard of identity: 100% malted barley from a single American distillery.
styles.ingredients: 100% malted barley.
styles.comments: Formalised by TTB in 2024 (27 CFR 5.144): mashed, distilled and matured in the United States at a single distillery; distilled to ≤80% ABV; matured in oak casks ≤700 L; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Unlike bourbon, the oak need not be new or charred.

styles.name: Rum (US standard)
styles.impression: Spirit from sugarcane products, ranging from light and clean to heavy and estery.
styles.ingredients: Sugarcane products — molasses, cane syrup, or cane juice.
styles.comments: 27 CFR 5.143: distilled from fermented sugarcane products at less than 95% ABV (190 proof) in such a manner that it possesses the taste, aroma and characteristics generally attributed to rum; bottled at ≥40% ABV. US law imposes no ageing requirement and no maximum congener limits, which is why 'rum' spans an enormous stylistic range.

styles.name: Rum (EU standard)
styles.impression: EU-regulated cane spirit with tighter congener requirements than the US definition.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 2019/787 Annex I(1): produced exclusively from molasses, cane syrup or cane juice; distilled at less than 96% ABV; minimum 225 g/hL of volatile substances at 100% ABV (a congener floor the US lacks); minimum 37.5% ABV. No added ethanol; sweetening only for rounding-off.
styles.comparison: The congener minimum means an EU 'rum' cannot be as neutral as some US-market products.

styles.name: Rhum Agricole (AOC Martinique)
styles.impression: Grassy, vegetal cane spirit distilled from fresh juice rather than molasses.
styles.ingredients: Fresh sugarcane juice only — never molasses.
styles.comments: AOC Martinique (1996): designated parcels on Martinique, specified cane varieties, fermentation without additives, single-column creole distillation to 65–75% ABV, bottled at ≥40%. Blanc rested ≥3 months; Élevé sous bois ≥12 months in oak; Vieux ≥3 years in oak ≤650 L.
styles.history: The style arose when 19th-century beet-sugar competition left cane juice available for direct distillation.

styles.name: Cachaça
styles.impression: Brazil's national spirit — fresh cane juice distilled to a comparatively low strength, retaining fruity and grassy character.
styles.ingredients: Fermented fresh sugarcane juice.
styles.comments: Brazilian Decree 6.871/2009 and MAPA Instruction 13/2005: produced in Brazil; distilled to 38–48% ABV (note the low maximum, which preserves congeners); up to 6 g/L sugar, or up to 30 g/L if labelled 'adoçada' (sweetened). Recognised as a distinctive product of Brazil by the US since 2013.

styles.name: Tequila
styles.impression: Cooked-agave spirit from designated Mexican regions, ranging from bright and peppery to oak-rounded.
styles.ingredients: Agave tequilana Weber, blue variety. '100% de agave' uses only agave sugars; 'mixto' permits up to 49% non-agave sugars.
styles.comments: NOM-006-SCFI-2012 and the Denominación de Origen: may be produced only in Jalisco and designated municipalities of Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit and Tamaulipas. Bottled at 35–55% ABV. Classes by ageing: Blanco (unaged or <2 months), Joven/Oro (blended or lightly aged), Reposado (≥2 months in oak), Añejo (≥1 year in oak ≤600 L), Extra Añejo (≥3 years).

styles.name: Mezcal
styles.impression: Agave spirit traditionally roasted in earthen pits, typically smoky and highly variable by species and maker.
styles.ingredients: Any agave species permitted by the standard — espadín, tobalá, tepeztate, madrecuishe and many others — not restricted to blue Weber.
styles.comments: NOM-070-SCFI-2016: produced in designated states including Oaxaca, Guerrero, Durango, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas, Michoacán, Puebla, Guanajuato and Tamaulipas. Bottled 35–55% ABV, always 100% agave. Three production classes: Mezcal (industrial methods permitted), Mezcal Artesanal (pit roasting, stone/wood milling, wood or clay stills), and Mezcal Ancestral (clay pot stills, most traditional throughout).
styles.comparison: All tequila is technically a mezcal in the historical sense, but the two now hold separate denominations of origin.

styles.name: Raicilla & Bacanora
styles.impression: Regional Mexican agave spirits with their own denominations of origin.
styles.comments: Bacanora (NOM-168, Sonora, from Agave angustifolia/pacífica) and Raicilla (DO granted 2019, Jalisco/Nayarit, from Agave maximiliana and others) were long produced informally — bacanora was outright prohibited in Sonora from 1915 to 1992 — and are now legally protected categories.

styles.name: Cognac
styles.impression: Double-distilled French grape brandy of great finesse, oak-matured.
styles.ingredients: Predominantly Ugni Blanc, with Folle Blanche and Colombard permitted.
styles.comments: AOC Cognac: grapes grown and distilled within the Charente/Charente-Maritime crus; double distillation in a copper alambic charentais, off the still at no more than 72.4% ABV; matured in French oak; bottled at ≥40% ABV. Age grades count from 1 April following harvest: VS ≥2 years, VSOP ≥4 years, Napoléon ≥6 years, XO ≥10 years (raised from 6 in 2018).

styles.name: Armagnac
styles.impression: Gascon grape brandy, typically column-distilled once and more rustic and aromatic than Cognac.
styles.comments: AOC Armagnac (Bas-Armagnac, Ténarèze, Haut-Armagnac): usually continuous distillation in the alambic armagnacais to a lower strength than Cognac, retaining more congeners; aged in Gascon or Limousin oak; ≥40% ABV. Vintage (millésime) bottlings are a far more common tradition than in Cognac.

styles.name: Calvados
styles.impression: Norman apple (and pear) brandy.
styles.ingredients: Cider apples, and up to 30% pears depending on the appellation.
styles.comments: Three AOCs: Calvados, Calvados Pays d'Auge (double pot distillation, ≥2 years) and Calvados Domfrontais (≥30% pears, column distillation, ≥3 years). Base cider fermented without added sugar; minimum 2 years in oak; ≥40% ABV.

styles.name: Pisco
styles.impression: Aromatic grape spirit from Peru or Chile — two distinct, legally separate products.
styles.comments: Peru (NTP 211.001): from eight permitted grape varieties in designated coastal regions; distilled to bottling strength with NO water added afterwards, no ageing in wood permitted (rest in inert vessels ≥3 months), 38–48% ABV. Chile's DO permits water reduction and oak. The two nations dispute the name internationally.
styles.examples: Barsol, Macchu Pisco (Peru); Alto del Carmen (Chile)

styles.name: Grappa & Pomace Brandy
styles.impression: Spirit distilled from grape pomace — skins, seeds and stems left after winemaking.
styles.comments: EU Regulation 2019/787: 'Grappa' is reserved for pomace of grapes produced and distilled in Italy (with parallel protections for Grappa di Ticino, Marc de Champagne, Bagaceira, Orujo, Tsipouro/Tsikoudia). Distilled at less than 86% ABV; ≥37.5% ABV bottling.

styles.name: Fruit Brandy / Eau-de-Vie
styles.impression: Unaged or lightly aged spirit distilled from whole fruit, prized for varietal aroma.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: fermented from fruit flesh (with stones where traditional); distilled at less than 86% ABV; no added alcohol, colouring or flavouring; ≥37.5% ABV. Protected examples include Kirsch, Mirabelle, Poire Williams, Slivovitz and Calvados' cousins. US law defines a parallel 'fruit brandy' at ≥40% ABV.

styles.name: Gin
styles.impression: Neutral spirit flavoured with juniper as the dominant character.
styles.ingredients: Ethyl alcohol of agricultural origin plus juniper berries (Juniperus communis); other botanicals at the producer's discretion.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787 sets three tiers: 'Gin' (flavouring may be by any means, juniper predominant, ≥37.5% ABV); 'Distilled Gin' (redistilled with botanicals); and 'London Gin' (all flavour from redistillation of ethanol at ≥96% ABV with natural botanicals, no added colouring, sweetening ≤0.1 g/L, nothing added but water). US requires ≥40% ABV. Note that 'London Gin' is a method, not a place — it need not be made in London.

styles.name: Vodka
styles.impression: Spirit deliberately refined toward neutrality.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: ethanol of agricultural origin rectified so as to selectively reduce the organoleptic characteristics of the raw material; ≥37.5% ABV. US 27 CFR: treated with charcoal or otherwise so as to be without distinctive character, aroma, taste or colour; ≥40% ABV. The EU permits raw-material labelling; if made from anything other than cereals or potatoes, the base must be declared.

styles.name: Absinthe
styles.impression: High-strength anise and wormwood spirit, traditionally louching when diluted.
styles.ingredients: Grande wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), green anise, and fennel — the 'holy trinity'.
styles.comments: Absinthe has no harmonised EU spirit-category definition; it is regulated through thujone limits — EU: ≤35 mg/kg in bitter spirits; US TTB: 'thujone-free' meaning <10 ppm, and the label may not depict hallucinogenic or psychotropic effects. Switzerland's Absinthe/Fée Verte du Val-de-Travers holds a protected geographical indication. Typical bottling strength 45–74% ABV.
styles.history: Banned across much of Europe and the US in the early 20th century; legalised again in the EU from the 1990s and in the US in 2007.

styles.name: Aquavit / Akvavit
styles.impression: Scandinavian spirit dominated by caraway or dill.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: spirit drink flavoured with caraway seeds and/or dill seeds, distilled with botanicals; ≥37.5% ABV. Essential oils of other botanicals may contribute but caraway/dill must predominate. Norwegian Linie aquavit is traditionally matured in sherry casks shipped across the equator and back.

styles.name: Liqueur / Cordial
styles.impression: Sweetened flavoured spirit.
styles.comments: EU 2019/787: minimum 100 g/L sugar (lower thresholds for cherry and gentian liqueurs); ≥15% ABV. US 27 CFR: 'cordial/liqueur' requires ≥2.5% sugar by weight and flavouring from natural materials; ≥30 proof (15% ABV). Crème de cassis requires ≥400 g/L sugar in the EU.

styles.name: Baijiu
styles.impression: China's national spirit and the world's most-consumed by volume — solid-state fermented grain spirit with intense, distinctive aromatics.
styles.ingredients: Sorghum most typically, often with rice, glutinous rice, wheat or corn; saccharified and fermented by qū (麴) starter cultures carrying moulds, yeasts and bacteria.
styles.comments: Governed by Chinese GB/T national standards, which classify baijiu by aroma type (香型) rather than by region: strong/thick aroma (nóngxiāng), light aroma (qīngxiāng), sauce aroma (jiàngxiāng), rice aroma (mǐxiāng) and around a dozen others. Solid-state fermentation in earthen pits or stone vessels distinguishes it from nearly all Western spirits.

styles.name: Shochu & Awamori
styles.impression: Japanese distilled spirit, typically single-distilled and lower in strength than Western spirits.
styles.ingredients: Barley (mugi), sweet potato (imo), rice (kome), buckwheat or brown sugar; saccharified with kōji mould.
styles.comments: Japanese Liquor Tax Act distinguishes honkaku (single-distilled, 'authentic', ≤45% ABV) from korui (multiply-distilled, ≤36% ABV). Awamori is the Okinawan variant, made from long-grain Thai indica rice with black kōji (Aspergillus luchuensis); aged awamori is called kūsū.

styles.name: Soju
styles.impression: Korea's dominant spirit; modern mass-market soju is diluted and lightly sweetened.
styles.comments: Korean Liquor Tax Act separates distilled soju (증류식, from grain, retaining congeners) from diluted soju (희석식, neutral spirit cut with water and flavourings) — the latter accounts for the overwhelming majority of sales, typically bottled at 16–25% ABV. Traditional Andong soju is distilled and considerably stronger.

styles.name: Arrack, Feni & Palm Spirits
styles.impression: South and Southeast Asian spirits from palm sap, cashew apple or cane.
styles.comments: Ceylon Arrack is distilled from fermented coconut palm flower sap and is protected as a Sri Lankan product. Feni holds a Goan GI: cashew feni from cashew-apple juice, coconut feni from palm toddy, traditionally triple-distilled in earthen pots. Batavia arrack (Java) is cane-based with red rice cakes added to fermentation.

styles.name: Unaged Grain Spirit / 'Moonshine'
styles.impression: Clear, unaged spirit from a grain or sugar wash — the untaxed tradition, now sold legally under existing categories.
styles.comments: 'Moonshine' is a cultural term, not a US standard of identity. To be labelled legally a product must fall into an existing class: Corn Whiskey (≥80% corn, ≤80% ABV distillation, unaged or in used/uncharred oak); unaged 'whisky' generally (grain mash, <95% ABV); Neutral Spirits/Vodka if distilled ≥95% ABV; or a 'Distilled Spirits Specialty' if sugar-based or flavoured. Historically the term denotes illicit, untaxed production — which remains a federal offence regardless of the recipe.
styles.comparison: Sugar-wash 'moonshine' cannot legally be called whiskey at all, since whiskey requires a grain mash.
styles.examples: Ole Smoky, Sugarlands (sold as corn whiskey or specialty)
styles.tags: moonshine, white dog, unaged, corn whiskey
